beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: This is Rohan. First real job in Bengaluru, first salary, and today, the phone he has wanted for a whole year.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: It costs ₹60,000. He swipes his brand new credit card, and the bill says he only needs to pay ₹3,000 this month.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That one easy choice will keep him paying for 16 years. And this phone will end up costing him ₹1.7 L.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: One month later, his first credit card statement arrives.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Two numbers. Total due, ₹60,000. Minimum due, just ₹3,000. One feels like a lot of money. The other feels like nothing.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So Rohan does what most people do. He pays the minimum.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Done! Bill paid, phone sorted.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Rohan, do you know what the bank charges you on the rest?

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Nothing, right? I paid on time!

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Here is the catch. When you pay anything less than the total, interest starts on everything you still owe. Around 3.5% every single month.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: 3.5% a month sounds small. But over a year, that is 42%. A credit card is one of the most expensive ways to borrow money.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: And it compounds. This month's interest joins the balance, and next month you pay interest on that bigger number too. Like a snowball, rolling downhill.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: So every time Rohan pays, interest takes the first big bite. Only what is left actually shrinks his debt.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Twelve months go by. Rohan pays every single bill, on time.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: By now, he has paid ₹32,862. And he still owes ₹48,991.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: What? I have already paid more than half the phone!

lines.text: Lost to interest in year one

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: That is because ₹21,853 of what he paid went straight to interest. In just one year.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: If he keeps paying only the minimum, the balance falls painfully slowly. Because the minimum due shrinks every time the balance shrinks.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: It takes 194 months. That is 16 years. By the time it is paid off, Rohan will be shopping for his third new phone.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: In total, he pays ₹1.7 L for a ₹60,000 phone. 2.9× the price on the box.

beats.speaker: sharma
beats.say: In my bank days, we had a name for people who pay only the minimum. We called them our best customers.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: The minimum due is not there to help you. It is there to keep you paying.

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Here is what to do instead. Three simple things.

items.text: Pay the total due, every month
Can't? Convert it to an EMI
Use it like a debit card

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: One. Pay the total due every month, not the minimum. Set autopay for the full amount, so you never forget.

items.text: Pay the total due, every month
Can't? Convert it to an EMI
Use it like a debit card

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Two. If you really cannot pay it all, convert the purchase into an EMI. On this phone, a one year EMI at 16% costs about ₹5,326 in interest.

items.text: Pay the total due, every month
Can't? Convert it to an EMI
Use it like a debit card

beats.speaker: priya
beats.say: Three. Treat your credit card like a debit card. If the money is not in your account, do not swipe.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Same phone, three prices. Pay only the minimum, and the interest is ₹1.1 L. Convert to an EMI, about ₹5,326. Pay in full, and it costs nothing extra.

beats.speaker: rohan
beats.say: Total due. Paid. Every month.

params.cta: Pay the total due. Every month.
params.follow: Follow for one money idea a day
params.assumption: Assumes 3.5% a month interest and a minimum due of 5% of the balance. Real cards also add GST and fees.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.say: Real cards also charge interest from the day you buy, and add tax on top. So the true cost is even higher. Follow for one money idea, every day.
